newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks end up slightly on bargain-hunting.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks end up slightly on bargain-hunting.

text.p: Mexican stocks rebounded to close slightly up on Monday as local and foreign bottom-fishing buyers stepped in to buy, traders and analysts said.
"The rebound was slight. Foreign and local stepped in to snap up bargains and stragglers," said a trader at the Inverlat brokerage. "Trade was dull, however."
The leading IPC share index ended up 4.61 points, or 0.13 percent, at 3,685.17. Volume was light at 43.8 million shares traded.
Other dealers said the market still had upside potential despite intraday profit-taking.
"Although dealers have been taking profits, the market feels like it's going up. Money is still flowing in," one dealer said.
The broad market was at odds with the IPC, with decliners outnumbering gainers by 52 to 30, out of a total of 105 stocks traded.
Autoparts maker Isasa, up four centavos to 36 centavos, led the gainers' list after lagging the market, traders said.

Traders noted the presence of Mexico's "big three" financial groups among the decliners, Serfin B, Bancomer B and Banacci B, which closed down 19, eight and 54 centavos, respectively, at 3.29, 3.02 and 16.00 pesos.

"Financial stocks are being stirred up by new accountancy practices and past-due loans portfolio sales to the government. Furthermore, the market did not welcome Banacci's 1996 earnings report last week. There are some surprises in store for other financial groups," one trader said.
Mexico introduced accountancy practices more in line with international standards on Jan 1.
Traders said the new practices would increase estimates of past-due loans for banks.
The National Securities Commission announced on Jan 23 Banacci and Bancomer were to sell additional past-due loans portfolios for eight billion pesos each.
Banacci's banking arm posted 1996 earnings on Jan 24 that were down 33 percent in year-ago terms.
Traders said they saw a volatile session on Tuesday, coupled to developments on Wall Street and forecast interest rate movements for the weekly central bank primary auction.
